Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

Vignette:
Kiet's eyes still widened in terror when he recalled the sound of his own screams. It had been years since he was released from the detention center, but the memories lingered, refusing to be silenced. The torture sessions, in particular, replayed in his mind like a film on an endless loop – the feeling of helplessness, the searing pain, and the crushing fear that he would never escape. Even now, as a successful accountant, Kiet couldn't shake off the sense that these memories didn't truly belong to him; they felt like someone else's horror story, not his own. As he went about his day, mundane tasks could suddenly trigger a flashback – the smell of disinfectant in a public restroom, the sound of raised voices in a crowded street. Kiet would find himself back in that dingy cell, reliving the anguish and the despair. His mind would frantically try to re-order the events, but they remained stubbornly jumbled, like shards of broken glass that refused to be pieced together. Kiet had grown increasingly withdrawn since his divorce a year ago. He couldn't bear the thought of opening up to strangers, lest they discover the depths of his emotional scars. Even conversations with acquaintances felt like an ordeal; he would nervously scan their faces for any sign of distrust or revulsion. "What if they find out what happened to me?" he would think to himself, his mind racing with catastrophic scenarios. The future seemed like a minefield, full of unknown dangers and potential threats. Whenever someone asked him about his plans or aspirations, Kiet's anxiety spiked. He couldn't envision a life free from the shadows of his past; it was as if he was forever trapped in that detention center, waiting for the next blow to fall. As an accountant, Kiet was meticulous and detail-oriented, but his work had begun to suffer. His avoidance behaviors – skipping meetings, turning down social invitations – were starting to take a toll on his relationships with clients and colleagues. They noticed the change in him, but Kiet couldn't bring himself to confide in them; he felt like a fragile vase, liable to shatter at any moment. Kiet's greatest fear was that he would never be able to escape the darkness of his past. He believed that others would have been stronger, more resilient, and better equipped to cope with what he endured. The thought haunted him – "If only I had been braver, smarter, or quicker, maybe this wouldn't have happened." This conviction had become a constant companion, whispering doubts and recriminations in his ear. Lately, Kiet's world had shrunk to the size of his apartment. He avoided going out, afraid of encountering strangers who might ask too many questions or – worse still – recognize him from somewhere. The irony wasn't lost on him; he had survived torture, but it was the fear of being seen, truly seen, that now held him hostage. As Kiet sat in his dimly lit living room, surrounded by stacks of unopened bills and unread books, he realized that he couldn't keep running from his memories. He needed help to make sense of the chaos inside his head, to learn how to silence the echoes of the past, and to rebuild a life that felt authentic, not just borrowed. With a deep breath, Kiet picked up the phone and dialed the number of a therapist he had been putting off for months; it was time to confront the shadows head-on, no matter how daunting the prospect seemed.
